verses.text: Moses went and spoke these words to all Israel.
He said to them, “I am one hundred twenty years old today. I can no more go out and come in. Yahweh has said to me, ‘You shall not go over this Jordan.’
Yahweh your God himself will go over before you. He will destroy these nations from before you, and you shall dispossess them. Joshua will go over before you, as Yahweh has spoken.
Yahweh will do to them as he did to Sihon and to Og, the kings of the Amorites, and to their land; whom he destroyed.
Yahweh will deliver them up before you, and you shall do to them according to all the commandment which I have commanded you.
Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or scared of them; for Yahweh your God himself is who goes with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you.”

Moses called to Joshua, and said to him in the sight of all Israel, “Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land which Yahweh has sworn to their fathers to give them; and you shall cause them to inherit it.
Yahweh himself is who goes before you. He will be with you. He will not fail you nor forsake you. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be discouraged.”
Moses wrote this law, and delivered it to the priests the sons of Levi, who bore the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, and to all the elders of Israel.
Moses commanded them, saying, “At the end of every seven years, in the set time of the year of release, in the feast of tents,
when all Israel has come to appear before Yahweh your God in the place which he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel in their hearing.

Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and the foreigners who are within your gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn, and fear Yahweh your God, and observe to do all the words of this law;
and that their children, who have not known, may hear, and learn to fear Yahweh your God, as long as you live in the land where you go over the Jordan to possess it.”

Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, your days approach that you must die. Call Joshua, and present yourselves in the Tent of Meeting, that I may commission him.” Moses and Joshua went, and presented themselves in the Tent of Meeting.
Yahweh appeared in the Tent in a pillar of cloud, and the pillar of cloud stood over the Tent’s door.

Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, you shall sleep with your fathers. This people will rise up, and play the prostitute after the strange gods of the land, where they go to be among them, and will forsake me, and break my covenant which I have made with them.

Then my anger shall be kindled against them in that day, and I will forsake them, and I will hide my face from them, and they shall be devoured, and many evils and troubles shall come on them; so that they will say in that day, ‘Haven’t these evils come on us because our God is not among us?’
I will surely hide my face in that day for all the evil which they have done, in that they have turned to other gods.
“Now therefore write this song for yourselves, and teach it to the children of Israel. Put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the children of Israel.

For when I have brought them into the land which I swore to their fathers, flowing with milk and honey, and they have eaten and filled themselves, and grown fat; then they will turn to other gods, and serve them, and despise me, and break my covenant.

It will happen, when many evils and troubles have come on them, that this song will testify before them as a witness; for it will not be forgotten out of the mouths of their descendants; for I know their ways and what they are doing today, before I have brought them into the land which I swore.”
So Moses wrote this song the same day, and taught it the children of Israel.
He commissioned Joshua the son of Nun, and said, “Be strong and courageous; for you shall bring the children of Israel into the land which I swore to them. I will be with you.”
When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book, until they were finished,
Moses commanded the Levites, who bore the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, saying,
“Take this book of the law, and put it by the side of the ark of Yahweh’s covenant your God, that it may be there for a witness against you.
For I know your rebellion, and your stiff neck. Behold, while I am yet alive with you today, you have been rebellious against Yahweh. How much more after my death?
Assemble to me all the elders of your tribes, and your officers, that I may speak these words in their ears, and call heaven and earth to witness against them.

For I know that after my death you will utterly corrupt yourselves, and turn aside from the way which I have commanded you; and evil will happen to you in the latter days; because you will do that which is evil in Yahweh’s sight, to provoke him to anger through the work of your hands.”
Moses spoke in the ears of all the assembly of Israel the words of this song, until they were finished.

footnotes.content: Moses steps forward one last time to address the people, not with fresh revelation but with a review of what he's learned walking with God for forty years. There's something tender about how he chooses to spend his final breath—on words of encouragement rather than complaint or self-pity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred twenty—Moses speaks his age with clarity, not regret. He names the limit God has set: he will not cross the Jordan. There's a dignity in accepting what you cannot change and releasing it to the One who can. We're called to the same honest surrender.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses must know this stings—he's led them for forty years, and now Joshua will lead them in. Yet he speaks it plainly: the Lord goes before them. What a gift, to step aside and let others step forward under the same faithfulness that carried you. That's love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He calls to mind Sihon and Og—not as boasts but as reminders of God's power. These kings stood in the way, and God destroyed them. The implication is tender: what stood against your ancestors stands no longer. The God who conquered then conquers now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh will deliver them up before you." Moses speaks with absolute certainty about what has not yet happened. That's the tone of an old one who has learned the character of God so deeply that the future feels as solid as the past. His faith becomes their foundation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be strong and courageous." Moses repeats this like a grandparent's blessing—not because fear isn't real, but because God is realer. "He will not fail you nor forsake you." I've heard this promise in my own darkest hours, and found it true. You will too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses calls Joshua forward publicly, in sight of all Israel, and speaks his blessing into him. There's no hoarding of authority, no clinging to power. He names Joshua as the one God has chosen and commissions him with the people watching. That's what an elder leaves behind: a named successor and a watching community.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua hears the same words from the Lord himself—not filtered through Moses, but direct. "He will not fail you nor forsake you." There's mercy in repetition, especially when the weight lands heavy. Sometimes we need to hear the promise twice to let it settle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses writes down the law and gives it to the priests who bore the ark of the covenant. In an oral culture, writing itself is an act of stewardship—making sure the words won't be lost to time or faulty memory. Some things are too precious to rely on human recollection alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every seven years, the whole gathered people will hear the law read aloud. There's a rhythm to remembering—not constantly, but at appointed times, all together. Communities that forget who they are forget who they serve. That's why Moses builds in a cadence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The reading happens at the feast of tents, in the place God will choose—a holy time, a holy place, the whole nation listening together. There's power in that assembly. Hearing God's word together has always strengthened the weary and turned wanderers toward home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Men, women, children, even foreigners within your gates—all are gathered to hear and to learn to fear the Lord and keep His words. There's no hierarchy of belonging, no one too small or too strange to need His instruction. The covenant reaches everyone standing in that assembly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children who haven't yet known will hear and learn to fear God through the voices of their parents, generation after generation. That's how faith is passed down—not by book learning alone, but by being present when the Word is read, watching your elders bow before it and obey it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, your days approach that you must die." The Lord doesn't soften the truth. Death is coming for Moses, and there's no negotiation about it. But His next breath is about commissioning—"Call Joshua." Even as one door closes, another opens under God's hand. That's how He writes history.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The pillar of cloud—that same presence that led them through the wilderness for forty years—appears at the Tent of Meeting. The symbol of His constancy stands at the place of His covenant. Nothing is hidden; everything is witnessed. God is here, still, at the hinge of this transition.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God tells Moses plainly: after he sleeps, these people will turn to strange gods and break the covenant. He speaks the sorrow before it happens. A loving God doesn't hide hard truths from those He's trusting with leadership—He prepares them to weep what will come and keep faith anyway.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will hide my face from them." The consequence of turning away is that the Lord withdraws His presence, and they feel the weight of the world without His protection. But notice—He tells them this so they might learn it now, from the mouth of Moses, rather than learn it by falling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God says He will hide His face because they have turned to other gods. The connection is clear: unfaithfulness has a cost. But here's what I've learned—that hidden face is not permanent. In every generation, some remnant turns back and finds Him again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Write this song for yourselves, and teach it to the children." God commands a song—a way to sing the story, to embed the warning in something that can be remembered, hummed, passed down. Songs carry memory in a way bare facts never do. What we sing, we truly keep.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "When they have eaten and filled themselves, and grown fat." Prosperity is mentioned not as a blessing to celebrate but as a test—the hardest trial, often, for the faithful. Abundance whispers that we don't need God as much as we thought. That's the moment the song must be remembered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The song will testify as a witness—it will rise up in memory when they need it most, calling them back to their covenant and their God. There's deep kindness in this: God gives them His voice, embedded in music, so they can hear Him even when they've turned away. He makes it hard to forget.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses writes the song that same day and teaches it to the children. He doesn't delay, doesn't set it aside for a more convenient time. What God has commanded is done now. There's no hesitation in obedience—he'd learned that lesson long ago.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses commissions Joshua with the same words the Lord had spoken to him—not his own wisdom, but God's voice in his mouth. "I will be with you." The mantle passes, but the presence doesn't. Joshua stands not alone but in the company of the Almighty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses finishes writing the words of the law in a book—every word. It's a massive, meticulous act of stewardship. Not a summary, not a selection, but the whole covenant preserved for generations who haven't heard it from his lips. Some callings are just that: to write it down and leave it for others.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He commands the Levites who carried the ark to receive the law and place it beside the ark. The ones who bore God's presence are now entrusted with His words. There's a seamlessness—the law is woven into the heart of worship, not kept separate or treated as less sacred.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Put it by the side of the ark that it may be there for a witness against you." The law is positioned as both protection and testimony. It will guard them when they are faithful; it will witness against them when they turn away. God doesn't hide the terms of the covenant or pretend they don't matter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks plainly: "I know your rebellion and your stiff neck." Even now, while he stands among them, they have been rebellious. He doesn't soften it or pretend otherwise. An old shepherd who loves his flock tells them the hard truth because he knows what awaits without it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gathers the elders and officers and calls heaven and earth to witness. What a moment—the cosmos itself is called to be a witness to what God will say through His servant. This is no private conversation; this is covenant language, as weighty and binding as creation itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks prophecy—he knows they will corrupt themselves after he dies and turn aside from God's way. But he speaks it as warning, not as acceptance. His words are meant to shake them awake before it happens, to let them choose differently if they will. A prophet loves his people too much to stay silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks the words of the song to the assembly until they are finished. Readers today hear an echo in this—our own calling to hear and receive God's Word, passed down through centuries, still strong, still calling us back. What Moses sang, we continue to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
